narrative: The model estimates a 34% chance that you will fail your final year—roughly one in three. That does not mean failure is certain, but it is a meaningful risk, which is why the school is requiring remedial courses rather than waiting. The strongest influences on this estimate actually worked in your favor. Your record of zero past class failures was the most influential factor, and it lowered your risk; this matches the average among students who passed. Your intention to pursue higher education was the second most influential factor and also lowered risk; every passed student in the comparison shared that goal. Your father’s secondary education was third and likewise reduced risk, being a common background among passers. So the prediction is not driven by those strengths—they are protective. The model still flags you because other parts of your profile combine less favorably, especially very limited weekly study time, eight absences compared with an average of under four among passers, and high weekend alcohol use, which is uncommon among students who passed. To improve, treat the remedial courses as a structured chance to build a weekly study routine, attend every class to cut absences, and reduce weekend drinking. Use the family support and internet access you already have, and ask your teachers for specific targets so the risk is lowered before final exams.
